# On Tending a Digital Garden

A digital garden is the opposite of a blog. A blog is a *stream* — reverse-chronological,
performative, optimized for the moment of publishing and then forgotten. A garden is a
*topology* — a web of notes that grow, get pruned, and link to each other, optimized for
being revisited.

I started this place because my [[Evergreen Notes]] were dying in a private vault. Notes
want to be linked, and links want to be walked. Keeping them private was like growing
tomatoes in a sealed jar.

## The three rules I actually follow

1. **Plant ugly.** A note can go public the day it's a single sentence. The 🌰 seedling
   tag is permission to be wrong in public.
2. **Link before you file.** I never sort a note into a folder. I connect it to two or
   three others and let the structure emerge. This is the core idea I stole from
   [[Book — How to Take Smart Notes]].
3. **Tend on a schedule, not on inspiration.** Twenty minutes on Sunday. Re-read one old
   note, fix one link, pull one weed.

## Why "growth states" beat folders

Folders force a note to live in exactly one place. But [[Compost Is a Distributed System]]
is *equally* a gardening note and a systems note — forcing it into one bin loses the most
interesting thing about it: that it's both.

Growth states ("seedling / budding / evergreen") describe a note's *confidence*, which is
the dimension I actually want to track. A folder tells you where something is filed. A
ripeness tag tells you whether to trust it.

## The Stoic angle

There's a reason this practice agrees with me. Tending a garden is an exercise in
[[The Dichotomy of Control]]: I control whether I show up on Sunday and whether I link
honestly. I do *not* control whether anyone reads it, whether a note ages well, or whether
the idea was good. Detaching from the outcome is exactly what makes it sustainable.
